summary: RFC 7830 defines the EDNS(0) Padding option but not how much to pad. This experimental memo lists possible padding policies, discusses their implications, and recommends one option.

eli5.summary: Secret notes can be guessed from their size, so you add filler to make them look alike. This says how much filler to add.

questions: how much to pad dns messages
how much should dns messages be padded
what is block length padding for dns
subtitle: How much should a DNS message be padded? Block lengths of 128 bytes for queries and 468 for responses.

tldr.problem: RFC 7830 lets DNS clients and servers add padding to messages, but deliberately does not say how much. Encrypted DNS messages can still be correlated by their sizes.
tldr.mechanism: This memo compares padding policies and recommends Block-Length Padding: clients pad queries to a multiple of 128 octets, and servers pad responses to a multiple of 468 octets.
tldr.outcome: It is an experimental recommendation. Padding helps only on encrypted DNS transports, and it does not hide timing or the number of query and response pairs.

today: RFC 8467 is Experimental and has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 7830, which defines the Padding option itself.

sections.title: Why Padding Needs a Policy
sections.content:
RFC 7830 defines the EDNS(0) Padding option, which lets DNS clients and servers add a variable number of bytes to a message. The goal is to hamper size-based correlation of encrypted DNS messages. That RFC deliberately leaves the actual padding length open.

This memo fills the gap. It lists padding strategies, gives the advantages and disadvantages of each, and recommends one experimental strategy. Padding is useful only when the transport is encrypted, for example DNS over TLS (RFC 7858) or DNS over DTLS (RFC 8094).
sections.eli5: A padlock hides what is in a box, but not how big the box is. Padding makes boxes look more alike, and this memo says how to choose the extra size.

sections.title: General Guidance for Padders
sections.content:
The Padding option takes up message space, so it MUST be the last EDNS(0) option applied before a DNS message is sent. Where networks or devices are scarce (battery-powered devices, low bandwidth, high-cost links), the cost of bigger messages must be weighed against the gain in confidentiality.

The message size fed into any padding strategy MUST be calculated without the extra 2-octet length field that TCP transport adds. Otherwise the padded size would differ between transports and leak a hint of the original length. The RFC's example: with a block length of 32 octets, a 59-octet message is padded to 64 octets over UDP, but if the 2 extra octets were counted (61 in total) it would grow to 96 octets, because the Padding option is at least 4 octets long.
sections.eli5: Always put the filler in last, and measure the note the same way no matter which mail truck carries it. Otherwise the size gives the secret away again.

sections.title: The Recommended Block-Length Strategy
sections.content:
In Block-Length Padding, a sender pads each message so its padded length is a multiple of a chosen block length. This sharply reduces the variety of message sizes. Based on empirical research by Daniel K. Gillmor, the RFC says padding SHOULD follow this strategy:

  • Clients SHOULD pad queries to the closest multiple of 128 octets.
  • A server that receives a query with the Padding option MUST pad the response, and SHOULD pad it to a multiple of 468 octets.

This applies only if the DNS transport is encrypted. Even a zero-length Padding option adds 4 octets, which implementors must account for.

The research simulated padding on real traffic from busy recursive resolvers. It scored each policy by a cost to the attacker (the share of query and response pairs landing in the same size bucket) and a cost to the defender (the size factor between padded and unpadded messages). A 128-byte block for queries and a 468-byte block for responses was the best trade-off. 468 was chosen so that 3 blocks of 468 octets still fit comfortably into typical MTU values.

The strategy is easy to implement and needs no random numbers. Its weakness is that the block size is public, so the minimum length of the unpadded message can be inferred. Large blocks may cause UDP fragmentation if a multiple of the block does not fit the MTU. The RFC also notes that once DNSSEC-validating clients become more common, size patterns may change and the recommendation may need revisiting.
sections.eli5: Imagine only shipping boxes in a few fixed sizes. A small note goes in the small box, a bigger one in the next size up, so outsiders can only tell which size box it is.

sections.title: Other Strategies and Ones to Avoid
sections.content:
Maximal-Length Padding pads every message to the maximum size negotiated. It gives the highest message-size confidentiality, but it is wasteful and often exceeds the MTU, causing fragments and lower delivery odds over UDP. It is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Random-Length Padding adds a random amount of padding. An attacker who sees many requests can infer the original length from the distribution of total lengths, and limited data shows it exposes slightly more entropy than Block-Length Padding. It is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Random-Block-Length Padding randomly picks among a few block lengths and then applies block padding. It gives more variety in sizes but takes more effort to implement, and the RFC says it needs further empirical study.

Appendix A lists two policies that are not sensible. No Padding MUST NOT be used unless fewer than 4 octets remain for the option. Fixed-Length Padding adds a constant amount, which is easily discovered, so it MUST NOT be used except for test applications.
sections.eli5: Filling every box to the max wastes space, and random filler can be averaged out by a patient watcher. Never adding filler, or always the same amount, hides nothing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The policy and its parameters have a significant effect on how well encrypted DNS resists size-based correlation attacks. Implementors must consider which policies to offer, the default policy, which parameters are configurable and their defaults.

A client's effort can be undone if the server pads responses poorly, so a client may want a server whose response padding is at least as effective. Even with encryption and padding it may be trivial to tell the traffic is DNS, and padding does not stop leaks through timing or the number of query and response pairs. Cover traffic or response jitter could help, but the RFC calls them out of scope and says there is not enough analysis or data to recommend them. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Hiding the size is only one trick. Someone could still watch when notes are sent and how many, so padding is not a complete cloak.
